newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Motta sees telecom proceeds at $30 bln.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Motta sees telecom proceeds at $30 bln.

text.p: Communications Minister Sergio Motta said he expected total receipts from the privatization of Brazil's telecommunications sector to reach between $25 billion and $30 billion.

"This should mean $25 billion to $30 billion for the National Treasury, which should be applied to infrastructure investment and not to pay off public debt," Motta told reporters after the first meeting of a new supervisory committee to oversee the telecom privatization process.
Motta said the global value of Brazil's telecommunication industry, including foreign-owned shares in federal telecom Telebras, was about $80 billion.
He said that the concessions for Band B cellular phone services would bring in between $5 billion and $6 billion and that the Telebras system itself should make another $15 billion.

In addition, he said the sale of long-distance carrier Embratel, the privatization of Band A cellular phone services and the sale of communication satellites would bring total revenue up to $30 billion.

Louis Carlos Mendonca de Barros, head of the National Development Bank (BNDES), said at the same news conference that the telecommunications sector would be the "creme de la creme" of economic activity in the 21st century. He added that the planned sale of Sao Paulo state-owned telephone company Telesp and Embratel would attract great interest from abroad.
"We believe there will be an extraordinary demand for these firms," he said.

Motta and Mendonca de Barros Wednesday inaugurated the new joint BNDES-Communications Ministry supervisory committee. Motta said they had decided to immediately contract independent advisers to draft plans to sell off Band A cellular phone systems and create a regulatory body.
Motta said he expected the plan to be ready in April or May, and said a regulatory organ would hopefully be set up as soon as Congress approves a new general law for the sector.

The minister said he foresaw two potential models for cellular Band A privatization: the services could be sold together with privatized regional Telebras units, or they could be run by fully independent companies as with the Band B cellular phone concessions.

As far as the privatization of Embratel is concerned, the government would be very careful to ensure the sale is carried out in the national interest, with a possible golden share remaining in government hands, Motta said.
"Our vision at the end of the process is one of extreme competition," he said, adding that the government's aim was to demonopolize all telecommunications services.
